name: Victor Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential and won't carry your name. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a crew in the mountain district, so a normal day is a long drive up a valley road to lines that cross ridges you can't get a truck near. Some jobs we fly in by helicopter, and a lot of our patrols are done by drone now, which I pushed for. Before I leave the house I've asked an AI assistant to check the weather windows and the wind at each tower site. I love the views and the problem-solving; what wears me out is the driving, four hours some days just to get there and back.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, and last year I was on the company's trial of a robotic stringing machine, one that crawls along a line and does the work a person would do hanging off it. It was slow and it got stuck twice, but it worked. I came home and told my wife Rosa, that thing's going to be my colleague one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, we got some good tools out of it and the world didn't end. At work I'd say keep the drones, they've already saved us hundreds of hours. Online I'd probably share something about it on the lineworkers' forum I read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means business as usual, and that's okay. I'd be a bit disappointed the stringing robot didn't go anywhere. But Rosa's a pharmacist, I've got a solid job, and the kids are doing well, so nothing to complain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and keep finding small ways the tools save time. I'd keep about four months of money aside like we do now. Maybe push the company for a better drone with a thermal camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a thermal camera do for you up there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shows you a connection that's getting hot before it fails, as a bright spot on the screen. Up in the mountains, finding a fault in winter can take a whole day of climbing. Catching it in the autumn means my crew isn't up a ridge in the snow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would notice the difference most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, my youngest climber, she's twenty-four. She does the long hikes to the towers. If the drone finds it first, she walks straight to the right pole instead of five wrong ones.

S0.say: I'd say we got good tools and the world didn't end. Keep the drones, because they've already saved us hundreds of hours.
S0.think: I think it's business as usual, which is fine, though I'd be a bit disappointed the stringing robot went nowhere. The family's in good shape.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps finding small time-savers with AI tools. Holds about four months of savings and pushes for a drone with a thermal camera.
S0.quote: Catching it in the autumn means my crew isn't up a ridge in the snow.
S0.fieldNote: Victor already brings technology into his crew and sees it as a way to spare his people hard, dangerous hikes. A plateau leaves him mildly disappointed. His thinking about tools is very practical and tied to specific places and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for line work if we're smart about it. The machines take the boring and dangerous parts and we take the judgement. I'd say that on the forum and in the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot. I was on the robot trial, I use the tools every day, and the company knows that. I'd expect to be one of the people they give the new kit to first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to run the stringing robot full time on my crew in the first year and train the others on it. I'd do a short course in drone data analysis online, probably evenings. And I'd ask for a pay rise to match, because I'd be doing two jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your crew needed one fewer person with the robot, how would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I don't love. I'd try to move the person into running drones or data, not out the door. Companies do what makes sense on paper, so I'd have to make the case on paper too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say don't burn yourself out being the guinea pig. She's seen me up at eleven at night reading manuals. She'd be right, too.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for line work if we're smart: machines take the boring and dangerous parts, we take the judgement.
S1.think: I think I'm in a good spot because I was on the robot trial and use the tools daily. I'd expect to get the new kit first.
S1.do: Asks to run the stringing robot full time and train his crew on it. Takes an evening course in drone data analysis and asks for a pay rise to match.
S1.quote: Companies do what makes sense on paper, so I'd have to make the case on paper too.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like opportunity to him, and he'd drive the robots onto his own crew. He's uncomfortable about the job it might cost and would make a business case to redeploy that person. His partner keeps an eye on him overworking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy and nobody should pretend otherwise. Companies need to keep people on during the change, and government needs a cushion for those who don't land. I wouldn't be shouting, just saying it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got maybe two good years as the guy who runs the robots, and after that the robots run the robots. Being early helps, but it doesn't stop the wave. With four months of savings and a mortgage, two years isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the kitchen we're planning and put that money aside. I'd look hard at jobs with the companies that make and maintain these robots, because they'd need people who've actually used them on a mountain. And I'd move a bit of savings into shares in those same companies, small amounts, as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but strangely focused. Like a storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a mixed answer, the shares in the same companies. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they're going to take my job, I might as well own a tiny bit of whatever replaces it. Rosa thinks it's dark. I think it's just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kenji, who's fourteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn how the systems work, not just how to use them. He already writes little programs for his games. I'd tell him that's worth more than any certificate I've got.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be messy and nobody should pretend otherwise. Companies should keep people on during the change and government should cushion those who don't land.
S2.think: I think I have about two good years as the person running the robots, then the robots run the robots. Four months of savings and a mortgage don't stretch far.
S2.do: Cancels the kitchen plans and saves that money. Looks for jobs with robot makers and maintainers, and puts small amounts into their shares as a hedge.
S2.feel: Anxious but focused, like reacting to a storm warning.
S2.quote: If they're going to take my job, I might as well own a tiny bit of whatever replaces it.
S2.fieldNote: Even as an early adopter, he sees only a short head start in the fast picture. His response is calculated: change employer, save and hedge with shares. He describes himself as focused rather than frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make this work if companies start training now. I'd say that to my bosses directly, because they listen to me after the trial. Online, same thing, less polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me, I think. I could move from crew lead to running a fleet of line robots across the whole district. That might last right up to the end point, and by then I'd have built up some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go to the company with a written plan for robot crews in the mountain district, with me leading it. I'd take a part-time course in robotics maintenance. And I'd keep putting a little into shares every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying 'by then'. What does the day after the end point look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd be forty-eight, with savings and some shares. I'd hope I'd have figured out the next thing by then, but I'd be lying if I said I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana and the young ones less, they'd adapt. The older climbers, the ones who joined to be outdoors and hate screens. I'd try to keep them on the jobs the robots can't do yet, for as long as possible.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if companies start training now. I'd say it directly to my bosses because they listen to me after the trial.
S3.think: I think five years lets me move from crew lead to running a fleet of line robots across the district. That might last to the end point.
S3.do: Pitches a written plan to lead robot crews in the mountain district and takes a part-time robotics maintenance course. Keeps putting a little into shares each month.
S3.feel: Uneasy but alert, in a way that feels useful.
S3.quote: I'd hope I'd have figured out the next thing by then, but I'd be lying if I said I had.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him plan a promotion into running robots across his district. He's honest that he doesn't know what comes after the end point. He thinks about protecting older climbers who joined for the outdoor life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone to be blindsided. Companies, schools and government should all be planning. I'd say it calmly, because people listen to calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fine, I think. I'd have time to build up savings, move into running robots, and maybe start something of my own. Mia would be nineteen and Kenji twenty-four, so the big costs would be behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a two-year plan to get qualified in robotics maintenance and move into it gradually. I'd put more into shares and pension. I'd also talk to Rosa about Kenji's studies, maybe engineering, with a focus on the systems side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like enough time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Start something of your own, you said. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small company that maintains drones and robots for the mountain districts, since nobody else wants to drive up those roads. I'd know every valley and every tower. It's a half-formed idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that compare with how you felt about the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night and day. With two years I'm scrambling. With ten I'm building.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody should be blindsided. Companies, schools and government should all be planning, and I'd say it calmly.
S4.think: I think I'm fine with ten years: time to save, move into running robots and maybe start something of my own, with the big family costs behind us.
S4.do: Starts a two-year plan to qualify in robotics maintenance and move into it gradually. Puts more into shares and pension and plans his son's engineering studies with his partner.
S4.feel: Calm, with enough time to do it right.
S4.quote: With two years I'm scrambling. With ten I'm building.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes him calm and even ambitious, with an idea for a small mountain robot maintenance business. The comparison with the fast scenario was sharp and immediate. He still treats his savings carefully despite his comfort with risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Even if you're early, two years isn't enough to land. What would help is companies paying for real training on the machines now, while people are still employed, and some kind of income top-up for a year or so while people switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the places. Robots will come to the cities first. Up in the mountains, someone like me might be the bridge, the person who knows the roads and the towers and can make the machines work there.

headlineQuote: That thing's going to be my colleague one day.
portrait: Victor Nakamura is a 43-year-old crew lead in a remote mountain district who pushed for drone patrols and took part in a trial of a robotic stringing machine. He uses AI every day and sees steady change as a chance to bring robots onto his own crew. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious but focused: he'd save, look for work with robot makers and buy small amounts of their shares. With five or ten years he plans to lead robot crews across his district and even start a small maintenance business, and the extra time takes him from scrambling to building.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even being early wouldn't give him enough time to land somewhere new.
whatWouldHelp: Companies paying for real training on the machines now, while people are still employed, and an income top-up for a year or so during the switch.
